Chapter 3 · Analytical formulas: a map of the PGSE parameter space

© 2026 Chantal Tax. All rights reserved. Shared for viewing only; not licensed for reuse or redistribution. Course: simulating the diffusion MRI signal. Chapter 2 computed the signal exactly, for any gradient. This chapter asks where it has a closed form. What you'll take away
  1. A PGSE experiment in a pore is fixed by three dimensionless numbers, ||(D\Delta/L^2||), ||(D\delta/L^2||) and ||(\gamma gL^3/D||). Every closed formula lives in one corner of this box.
  2. On the narrow-pulse face the signal is ||(\langle e^{iqX}\rangle||). The ||((q,t)||) map has four regions: free diffusion, short times (surface-to-volume ratio), long times (the pore form factor and diffraction), and the region where cumulants work.
  3. On the long-pulse face the ||((g,T)||) map has three regimes, free diffusion, motional narrowing and localisation, which meet at a triple point.
  4. Inside the box, for real PGSE sequences: how the edge of the cumulant region moves with ||(\delta/\Delta||), and a rule for it, tested against the exact signal.
  5. Two extra axes: walls that relax magnetization (Brownstein–Tarr) and exchange between compartments (Kärger).
  6. A one-page crib sheet with every formula, each one checked against the exact solutions of Chapter 2.
Every exercise has hints and a worked answer, folded away. Try the exercise first, then open the hint, then the answer.

The course at a glance

Ch Topic Status
1 Foundations: notation, diffusion equation, interface and boundary conditions, eigenmodes, displacement cumulants; Bloch–Torrey; the full multi-compartment problem and its weak form; length scales; Feynman–Kac done
2 Series expansions: matrix methods (MCF, multiple propagator, number of modes) and the cumulant expansion (Gaussian phase, kurtosis, finite pulses) done
3 Analytical formulas: the PGSE box, the narrow-pulse ||((q,t)||) map, the long-pulse ||((g,T)||) map, the inside of the box, relaxing walls and exchange this notebook
4 Grids and meshes: the method of lines, finite differences, time stepping and stability, periodic cells, finite elements, curved walls done
5 Monte Carlo: simulating the random walk coming
Units: lengths in µm, times in ms, gradients in mT/m, ||(\gamma = 2.6752\times10^{-4}||) rad/(ms·mT/m·µm). ||(D = 2||) µm²/ms throughout. Running example: a slab of width ||(L = 8||) µm with the gradient across it, so ||(L^2/D = 32||) ms. Where a formula exists for cylinders and spheres too, it is given alongside. How to read this chapter. Each section gives a formula, the region where it holds, and a figure that computes that region by comparing the formula with the exact signal of Chapter 2. 3.0 · The PGSE box

A PGSE sequence in a pore has five dimensional inputs: ||(\Delta||), ||(\delta||), ||(g||), the pore size ||(L||) and the diffusivity ||(D||). Only three dimensionless combinations matter. The natural units are the pore size for length and the pore time ||(L^2/D||) for time:
Number Definition As a ratio of lengths Running example (||(\delta = 10||), ||(\Delta = 20||) ms, ||(G = 205||) mT/m)
diffusion time ||(\tilde\Delta = D\Delta/L^2||) ||((\ell_\Delta/L)^2||), with ||(\ell_\Delta = \sqrt{D\Delta}||) 0.63
pulse duration ||(\tilde\delta = D\delta/L^2||) ||((\ell_\delta/L)^2||) 0.31
gradient strength ||(\Gamma = \gamma gL^3/D||) ||((L/\ell_g)^3||) 14.0, so ||(\ell_g = 3.3||) µm
The box is the set ||(0 < \tilde\delta \le \tilde\Delta||), ||(\Gamma > 0||). It has two faces where the physics simplifies:
  • The narrow-pulse face, ||(\tilde\delta\to0||). With ||(\Gamma\tilde\delta = \gamma g\delta L = qL||) held fixed, the gradient and the pulse length merge into one number, ||(q = \gamma g\delta||). The face is the ||((q,t)||) plane (Section 3a).
  • The long-pulse face, ||(\tilde\delta = \tilde\Delta||). The two lobes touch, and the effective gradient is ||(+g||) for ||(T/2||) and then ||(-g||) for ||(T/2||), with ||(T = 2\delta||). This is a spin echo in a constant gradient. The face is the ||((g,T)||) plane (Section 3b).
Real sequences sit inside the box (Section 3c). The sliders below place a sequence in it.

data.text/markdown:
3a · The narrow-pulse face: the ||((q,t)||) map

From the path picture to ||(\langle e^{iqX}\rangle||)

Suppose both gradient pulses are so short that spins do not move while they are on. The first pulse gives each spin the phase ||(\gamma g\delta\,x(0)||). After the refocusing pulse, the second removes ||(\gamma g\delta\,x(\Delta)||). So ||(\varphi = -qX||), with ||(q = \gamma g\delta||) and the displacement ||(X = x(\Delta) - x(0)||), and ||[E(q,\Delta) = \big\langle e^{iqX}\big\rangle = \int \bar P(X,\Delta)\,e^{iqX}\,dX ,||]the characteristic function of the displacement: the Fourier transform of the average propagator ||(\bar P||) of Chapter 1 (Stejskal & Tanner 1965; Tanner & Stejskal 1968). In powers of ||(q||), the cumulants of ||(\ln E||) are exactly the displacement cumulants, ||(\langle X^2\rangle||), ||(K(t)||), …. With finite pulses this identity breaks, because the phase then depends on the whole path, not only on its two end points (Chapter 2, Exercise 6). → When is a pulse narrow? A spin must not move far during a pulse compared with the two lengths the signal resolves: ||(\sqrt{D\delta} \ll L||) and ||(\sqrt{D\delta} \ll 1/q||). In addition ||(\delta \ll \Delta||).

The exact narrow-pulse signal of a slab

Put the eigenmode propagator of Chapter 1 into the Fourier integral. Every mode contributes its own decay ||(e^{-D\lambda_nt}||), weighted by how strongly it overlaps with the phase pattern ||(e^{iqx}||): ||[E(q,t) = \sum_n \frac{\lvert\tilde u_n(q)\rvert^2}{L}\,e^{-D\lambda_nt},\qquad \tilde u_n(q) = \int_0^L u_n(x)\,e^{iqx}\,dx .||]For a slab this gives the closed form of Tanner & Stejskal (1968): ||[E(q,t) = \frac{2\,(1-\cos qL)}{(qL)^2} + 4\,(qL)^2\sum_{n\ge1} e^{-n^2\pi^2Dt/L^2}\;\frac{1-(-1)^n\cos qL}{\big[(qL)^2-(n\pi)^2\big]^2}.||]It depends on ||(qL||) and ||(Dt/L^2||) only: these are the two coordinates of the narrow-pulse face. The first term is the ||(t\to\infty||) limit. The sum, which dies out on the pore time ||(\tau_1 = L^2/(\pi^2D)||), carries all the dynamics. Chapter 2's MCF reproduces it as ||(\delta\to0||); the check below uses ||(\delta = 0.05||) ms.

data.text/html: ① Propagator. ||(P(x\mid x_0,t) = \sum_n u_n(x)u_n(x_0)e^{-D\lambda_nt}||) (Chapter 1). ② Average over starting points. Spins start uniformly, with density ||(1/L||): ||[E = \frac1L\int_0^L\!\!\int_0^L P(x\mid x_0,t)\,e^{iq(x-x_0)}\,dx\,dx_0 = \frac1L\sum_n e^{-D\lambda_nt}\Big(\int u_n(x)e^{iqx}dx\Big)\Big(\int u_n(x_0)e^{-iqx_0}dx_0\Big) .||]⇒ The modes are real, so the second integral is the complex conjugate of the first: ||(E = \sum_n e^{-D\lambda_nt}\lvert\tilde u_n(q)\rvert^2/L||). ③ Mode ||(n = 0||). ||(\tilde u_0 = (e^{iqL}-1)/(iq\sqrt L)||), so ||(\lvert\tilde u_0\rvert^2/L = 2(1-\cos qL)/(qL)^2 = \operatorname{sinc}^2(qL/2)||). ④ Modes ||(n\ge1||). Write ||(\cos k_nx = \frac12(e^{ik_nx}+e^{-ik_nx})||) with ||(k_n = n\pi/L||), and integrate: ||[\tilde u_n = \sqrt{\tfrac2L}\;\frac{iq\,\big[1-(-1)^ne^{iqL}\big]}{k_n^2-q^2} ,\qquad \frac{\lvert\tilde u_n\rvert^2}{L} = \frac{2q^2\,\big[2-2(-1)^n\cos qL\big]}{L^2\,(k_n^2-q^2)^2} = \frac{4(qL)^2\,\big[1-(-1)^n\cos qL\big]}{\big[(qL)^2-(n\pi)^2\big]^2}.||]→ At ||(q = 0||) only ||(n = 0||) survives, with weight 1, so ||(E = 1||). ✓ → Every term is non-negative. The narrow-pulse echo of a closed pore can approach zero but never becomes negative. That is no longer true for finite pulses. → Same structure as the MSD weights of Chapter 1: there the weights were ||(\lvert\int u_n\,x\rvert^2||), here they are ||(\lvert\int u_n\,e^{iqx}\rvert^2||). Expanding ||(e^{iqx}||) in powers of ||(q||) turns one into the other.

The white band between the cumulant region and the form-factor region, around ||(qL \approx 2\pi||) at intermediate times, is where no closed formula works. It is exactly where diffraction is still forming. The next four subsections derive each formula and its region.

① Short times: free diffusion, the ||(b||)-matrix, and the surface-to-volume ratio

Free diffusion. Far from any wall ||(\bar P||) is a Gaussian of variance ||(2Dt||), so ||(E = e^{-q^2Dt}||). For narrow pulses ||(b = q^2\Delta||); for finite pulses ||(b = q^2(\Delta-\delta/3)||) (Stejskal & Tanner 1965). In an anisotropic medium the Gaussian has a covariance ||(2\mathbf Dt||) and ||[E = e^{-\mathbf b:\mathbf D} = \exp\Big(-\sum_{ij}b_{ij}D_{ij}\Big),\qquad b_{ij} = q_iq_j\,t ,||]the ||(b||)-matrix of DTI (Basser, Mattiello & LeBihan 1994). Your notes: the anisotropic membrane diffusion ||(D_{11}\ll D_{22}||) of the physiology course is this tensor. Walls, to first order. At short times only spins within about ||(\ell_D||) of a wall notice it, and they move less. Their fraction is proportional to the surface-to-volume ratio ||(S/V||), which gives the result of Mitra, Sen, Schwartz & Le Doussal (1992) and Mitra, Sen & Schwartz (1993): ||[\frac{D(t)}{D} = 1 - \frac{4}{3\sqrt\pi\,d}\,\frac SV\,\sqrt{Dt} + O(t),||]in ||(d||) dimensions, for any pore shape. Slab: ||(S/V = 2/L||), ||(d = 1||). Cylinder (in the cross-section): ||(S/V = 2/R||), ||(d = 2||). Sphere: ||(S/V = 3/R||), ||(d = 3||). The first measurements of ||(S/V||) this way were in porous media (Latour et al. 1993). The kurtosis appears at the same order. A slab at short times is a mixture: a bulk that diffuses freely, and a thin layer at each wall whose displacements are narrower. A mixture of Gaussian-like distributions of different widths has positive excess kurtosis. Exercise 2 derives, for a slab, ||[K(t) \approx \frac{16}{5\sqrt\pi}\,\frac{\sqrt{Dt}}{L} = 1.805\,\frac{\sqrt{Dt}}{L}.||]Edge enhancement. The same physics, seen locally: the right-hand panel shows the signal of each starting position ||(x_0||) across the slab. Spins near a wall are attenuated less, so in a high-resolution image the edges of a pore light up (Hyslop & Lauterbur 1991; Pütz, Barsky & Schulten 1992; de Swiet 1995).

data.text/markdown:
② Long times: closed pores, tortuosity and disorder

A closed pore. Once ||(\ell_D \gg L||), a spin has forgotten where it started. Its end point is uniform in the pore and independent of its start, so the displacement ||(X = x - x_0||) is the difference of two independent uniform positions. For a slab, ||(\bar P(X)||) is a triangle of half-width ||(L||): ||[\bar P(X) = \frac{L-\lvert X\rvert}{L^2},\qquad \langle X^2\rangle = \frac{L^2}{6},\qquad D(t) = \frac{\langle X^2\rangle}{2t} = \frac{L^2}{12\,t},\qquad K = -\frac35 .||]Its Fourier transform is the form factor of ③, ||(E = \operatorname{sinc}^2(qL/2)||). In a closed pore ||(D(t)||) falls to zero as ||(1/t||), and ||(K||) stays negative: the displacement is bounded, so the distribution has lighter tails than a Gaussian. → Motional narrowing is not on this face. "Motional narrowing" means the phase is averaged while the gradient is on. With ||(\delta\to0||) nothing is averaged during a pulse. The long-time narrow-pulse limit is the form factor; motional narrowing belongs to the long-pulse face (Section 3b). A connected medium. If spins can leave the pore, through permeable membranes or through gaps between obstacles, ||(D(t)||) does not go to zero but to a finite ||(D_\infty < D||). The ratio ||(D/D_\infty||) is the tortuosity. For a stack of membranes with spacing ||(L||) and permeability ||(\kappa||) (the interface condition of Chapter 1), the resistances to flux add in series (your notes: heat conduction through layers in series): ||[\frac1{D_\infty} = \frac1D + \frac1{\kappa L} .||]How ||(D(t)||) approaches ||(D_\infty||) carries the structure. Novikov et al. (2014) showed that the tail is a power law set by the type of disorder:
Structure Long-time approach Example
closed pore ||(D(t) \simeq L^2/(12t)\to0||) (slab) cell bodies, impermeable
periodic (ordered) ||(D(t) - D_\infty \propto 1/t||) a regular lattice of obstacles
short-range disorder in ||(d||) dimensions ||(D(t) - D_\infty \propto t^{-d/2}||) 1D: random beads or membranes along an axon, ||(t^{-1/2}||)
general ||(t^{-\vartheta}||), ||(\ \vartheta = (p + d)/2||) ||(p||) = structural exponent of the disorder
The ||(1/t||) of an ordered medium is the general constant offset in ||(\langle X^2\rangle = 2D_\infty t + c||). Short-range disorder decays more slowly, so it dominates. The ||(t^{-1/2}||) law along axons is what Burcaw et al. (2015) used to model ||(D(t)||) in white matter.

3c · Inside the box: real PGSE sequences

Between the two faces there are no new closed formulas. What remains is the question of Chapter 2: up to which gradient can I trust the Gaussian phase (cumulant) approximation? On the two faces the answer is known:
  • narrow pulses: ||(q\min(\ell_D, L)\lesssim1||) (Section 3a ④);
  • long pulses: the smallest of ||(\ell_D||) and ||(L||) must stay below about ||(\ell_g||) (Section 3b), i.e. ||(\min(\ell_D, L)/\ell_g\lesssim1||).
A rule of thumb to test. A natural guess for the interior is ||[H = \gamma gL\cdot\min\big(\delta,\ L^2/D\big)\ \lesssim\ 1 .||]It reads: the phase difference across the pore that builds up during one lobe, where the lobe counts only up to the pore time (after that the spins average over the pore). In dimensionless form ||(H = \Gamma\min(\tilde\delta, 1)||). For long pulses it gives ||(\Gamma = (L/\ell_g)^3\lesssim1||), the motional-narrowing edge. For narrow pulses it gives ||(qL\lesssim1||). A refinement. At short ||(\Delta||) the walls are hardly felt, and free diffusion is Gaussian at any gradient. So the length in the rule should be the one the spins actually explore, ||(\ell = \min(\sqrt{D\Delta}, L)||): ||[H_2 = \gamma g\,\ell\cdot\min\big(\delta,\ \ell^2/D\big)\ \lesssim\ 1,\qquad \ell = \min(\sqrt{D\Delta}, L).||]On the narrow-pulse face ||(H_2 = q\ell||), the cumulant boundary of 3a. On the long-pulse face ||(H_2 = (\ell/\ell_g)^3||), which gives both the free–localisation line (||(\ell_D = \ell_g||)) and the motional narrowing–localisation line (||(L = \ell_g||)) of 3b. The map shows the exact error of the GPA, ||(\lvert E_{\text{GPA}}/E - 1\rvert||), over the ||((L/\ell_g, \ell_\Delta/L)||) plane at a fixed ratio ||(\delta/\Delta||). 3d · Two extra axes

The box assumed reflecting, impermeable walls. Real walls can also remove magnetization (surface relaxation) or let it through (permeability). Each adds one dimensionless number and one more axis to the box.

① Relaxing walls: Brownstein and Tarr

If the wall relaxes magnetization with relaxivity ||(\rho||) (µm/ms), the reflecting condition of Chapter 1 becomes the Robin condition ||[D\,\frac{\partial m}{\partial n} + \rho\,m = 0\quad\text{on the wall}.||]The eigenmodes change, and with them the relaxation of the whole pore (Brownstein & Tarr 1979). For a slab, the slowest symmetric mode is ||(\cos\big(k(x - L/2)\big)||) with ||[\frac{kL}2\,\tan\frac{kL}2 = \frac{\rho L}{2D},\qquad \frac1{T_{2,\text{surf}}} = Dk^2 .||]The new axis is ||(\rho L/D||), which compares how fast the wall removes spins with how fast diffusion brings them there:
||(\rho L/D||) Regime Rate of the slowest mode Decay
||(\ll1||) fast diffusion (surface-limited) ||(\rho\,S/V||) (||(= 2\rho/L||) for a slab) one exponential
||(\gg1||) slow diffusion (diffusion-limited) ||(D\pi^2/L^2||) several exponentials
The fast-diffusion limit is why NMR relaxometry measures ||(S/V||) in rocks and why relaxation and pore size are linked (Brownstein & Tarr 1979). For diffusion MRI, relaxing walls take spins out of the layer next to the wall, the same layer that carries the short-time correction ① and the localisation signal of 3b. Mitra et al. (1993) show that ||(\rho||) enters ||(D(t)||) at order ||(t||).

② Exchange between compartments: Kärger

Now let two compartments exchange spins across a membrane. If the membrane is the bottleneck, each compartment is well mixed and can be described by one number, its magnetization. With narrow pulses, and a Gaussian signal inside each compartment, the two magnetizations obey a linear ODE system (Kärger 1985): ||[\frac{d\mathbf m}{dt} = -\big(q^2\mathbf D + \mathbf K\big)\,\mathbf m,\qquad \mathbf D = \begin{pmatrix}D_1&0\\0&D_2\end{pmatrix},\quad \mathbf K = \begin{pmatrix}k_1&-k_2\\-k_1&k_2\end{pmatrix},||]with ||(\mathbf m(0) = (p_1, p_2)||) and detailed balance ||(k_1p_1 = k_2p_2||). The signal is ||(E = (1,1)\,e^{-(b\mathbf D + \mathbf K\Delta)}\,\mathbf p||), with ||(b = q^2\Delta||). Your notes: a linear system ||(\dot{\mathbf x} = A\mathbf x||), solved by ||(e^{tA}||) and its eigenvalues, as on your ODE sheets. The new axis is ||(\Delta/\tau_{\text{ex}}||), with ||(1/\tau_{\text{ex}} = k_1 + k_2||). From Chapter 1, a barrier-limited membrane with permeability ||(\kappa||) gives ||(k_1 = \kappa\,(S/V)_1||). → Chapter 1 already contains this model as a set of slab modes (the permeable-membrane figure and Exercise 9). With a membrane in the middle of a slab, the uniform mode stays, and the slowest odd mode, one half high and the other low, decays at ||(D\lambda\approx4\kappa/L||). That is ||(k_1 + k_2||): each half has ||(S/V = 2/L||), so ||(k_1 = k_2 = 2\kappa/L||). Kärger's two magnetizations are the projections on these two modes; the faster modes, which he neglects, are the ones that need ||(\kappa L/D\ll1||) to die out first. The model needs ||(\kappa L/D\ll1||) (the same condition as for tortuosity in ②), and each compartment must be inside its own cumulant region (3a ④). Filter-exchange imaging (FEXI) measures ||(\tau_{\text{ex}}||) this way (Lasič et al. 2011).

Implementations

  • Closed-form compartment models. Camino and dmipy implement the cylinder and sphere signals of this chapter in their narrow-pulse (Stejskal–Tanner), Callaghan and Gaussian-phase forms, for fitting axon-diameter and cell-size models. Before fitting one, evaluate ||(H_2||) for the protocol (Exercise 8).
  • The exact references. The MCF of Chapter 2 (for example MCFAL, MISST, the cylindrical-surface code) computes the signal everywhere in the box, including the white bands of the maps.
  • Validating simulators. The closed forms are the standard checks for numerical simulators. A recent example: the "replay packs" of Fick (2026) store Monte Carlo walker histories so that any sequence can be computed later as a cheap inner product. They are checked against analytical solutions in pores before realistic axon meshes. Chapter 5 returns to this paper.
